title: Simple Linear Regression and Correlation

blocks.x: Many problems ask how two variables are related: the strength of a weld and its temperature, or the fuel use of a car and its weight. An empirical model is an equation fitted to observed data. It describes the relationship but is not derived from first principles.
In regression, the response $Y$ is random. The regressor $x$ is a value we choose, or measure with negligible error.
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\varepsilon.
$\beta_0$ (intercept) and $\beta_1$ (slope) are unknown regression coefficients.
$\varepsilon$ is a random error with $\Exp[\varepsilon]=0$ and $\Var[\varepsilon]=\sigma^2$.
For data $(x_i,y_i)$, $i=1,\dots,n$: $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$, with independent errors.
For inference we also assume normal errors: $\varepsilon_i\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$.
For a fixed $x$, three things follow:
$\Exp(Y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x$: the mean response lies on a straight line.
$\Var(Y\mid x)=\sigma^2$: the spread is the same at every $x$.
$\beta_1$ is the change in the mean response for one unit increase in $x$.
We use these $n=8$ observations throughout the chapter.

blocks.caption: The least squares line minimises the sum of squared vertical distances (dashed) from the data points to the line.

blocks.x: The method of least squares
We choose the line that is closest to the data, in the sense of the smallest sum of squared vertical deviations:
L(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\big)^2.
Setting $\partial L/\partial\beta_0=0$ and $\partial L/\partial\beta_1=0$ gives the least squares normal equations:
n\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\sum x_i=\sum y_i,\qquad\hat\beta_0\sum x_i+\hat\beta_1\sum x_i^2=\sum x_iy_i.
\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}.
The fitted line is $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x$. The residuals are $e_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i$. The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$.

The first normal equation gives $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$. Put this into the second: $\hat\beta_1\big(\sum x_i^2-n\bar{x}^2\big)=\sum x_iy_i-n\bar{x}\bar{y}$, that is, $\hat\beta_1S_{xx}=S_{xy}$. The function $L$ is a convex quadratic, so this point is a minimum.
The fitted line is $\hat{y}=0.0357+1.9976\,x$. Each unit increase in $x$ raises the mean response by about $2.0$.
Estimating $\sigma^2$
We estimate the error variance from the residuals.
$SS_E=\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2=\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$, and
\hat\sigma^2=MS_E=\frac{SS_E}{n-2}.
A convenient formula is $SS_E=S_{yy}-\hat\beta_1S_{xy}$.

The divisor $n-2$ is the degrees of freedom. Two parameters ($\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$) were estimated from the data, so two degrees of freedom are used up. With this divisor, $\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$.

sections.title: Properties of the Least Squares Estimators

blocks.x: Write $\hat\beta_1=\sum c_iY_i$ with $c_i=(x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}$. The $x_i$ are fixed, so $\hat\beta_1$ is a linear combination of the independent $Y_i$.
Under the model assumptions:
$\Exp[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$;
$\Exp[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2\Big(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)$;
$\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$;
if the errors are normal, then $\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1$ are normal, and $(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-2}$, independent of $(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)$.
The estimated standard errors are $\se(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$ and $\se(\hat\beta_0)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})}$.
(i) Since $\sum c_i=0$ and $\sum c_ix_i=1$, we get $\Exp[\hat\beta_1]=\sum c_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\beta_1$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\sum c_i^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$.
(ii) $\hat\beta_0=\bar{Y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$. The terms $\bar{Y}$ and $\hat\beta_1$ are uncorrelated (because $\sum c_i=0$), so $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2/n+\bar{x}^2\sigma^2/S_{xx}$.
(iii) and (iv) are proved in matrix form in Chapter 6 (Theorem 6.8). The residual vector lies in an $(n-2)$-dimensional space.

Among all linear unbiased estimators of $\beta_1$ (those of the form $\sum a_iY_i$), the least squares estimator $\hat\beta_1$ has the smallest variance. The same holds for $\hat\beta_0$. So the least squares estimators are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUE). This needs only uncorrelated errors with equal variance, not normality.
$\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$ is small when:
the noise $\sigma$ is small;
$n$ is large;
the $x$-values are spread out (large $S_{xx}$).
In a designed experiment, put the $x$ values at the ends of the range. Half at each end gives the largest $S_{xx}$. Add a few middle points to detect curvature.
Do not extrapolate. The fitted line says nothing about whether the relationship stays linear outside the data.

sections.title: Some Comments on Uses of Regression (CD Only)

blocks.x: Regression is used for three jobs:
description: summarise a trend;
prediction: estimate the response at a new $x$ within the range of the data;
control: choose $x$ to reach a target $y$.
Cautions:
A fitted line is valid only for $x$ values in the range of the data.
A strong fit shows association, not causation.
The regression of $y$ on $x$ is not the regression of $x$ on $y$. The two lines differ unless the correlation is $\pm1$.
The model assumes $x$ is measured without error.
A few influential points can control the whole fit.

sections.title: Hypothesis Tests in Simple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Use of $t$-Tests
With normal errors, dividing each coefficient by its estimated standard error gives a $t$ statistic.

T=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_{1,0}}{\se(\hat\beta_1)}\sim t_{n-2}\ \text{ when }\beta_1=\beta_{1,0},\qquad T=\frac{\hat\beta_0-\beta_{0,0}}{\se(\hat\beta_0)}\sim t_{n-2}\ \text{ when }\beta_0=\beta_{0,0}.
To test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_{1,0}$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne\beta_{1,0}$, reject if $\abs{t_0}>t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}$.
The most important case is $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. This is the test for significance of regression.
Fail to reject $H_0$: there is no evidence of a linear relationship. Either $x$ explains little of $Y$ (the best estimate of $Y$ for every $x$ is $\bar{y}$), or the true relationship is not linear.
Reject $H_0$: $x$ helps explain $Y$. The straight line may be adequate, or it may be a good first approximation that a higher-order term would improve.
Also, $\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$ are not independent: $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=-\bar{x}\sigma^2/S_{xx}$.
For Example 5.5:
Slope: $\se(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{0.0325/42}=0.0278$ and $t_0=1.9976/0.0278=71.8$ with $6$ degrees of freedom. This is far beyond $t_{0.005,6}=3.707$, so reject $H_0:\beta_1=0$ ($P<0.0001$).
Intercept: $\se(\hat\beta_0)=\sqrt{0.0325(1/8+20.25/42)}=0.1405$ and $t_0=0.0357/0.1405=0.25$. There is no evidence that the intercept differs from $0$.

Oxygen purity $y$ (%) against hydrocarbon level $x$ (%), $n=20$. $S_{xx}=0.68088$ and $S_{xy}=10.17744$, so $\hat\beta_1=14.947$ and $\hat\beta_0=74.283$. The fitted line is $\hat{y}=74.283+14.947x$. At $x=1.00$ the predicted purity is $89.23\%$.

Test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ at $\alpha=0.01$: $t_0=11.35$ against $t_{0.005,18}=2.88$. Also $F_0=152.13/1.18=128.86=t_0^2$, with $P\approx1.2\times10^{-9}$. Reject. Finally $R^2=152.13/173.38=0.877$: the model explains $87.7\%$ of the variability.
Analysis of Variance Approach to Test Significance of Regression
The total variability in $y$ splits into a part explained by the regression and a part left over.
\underbrace{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}_{SS_T=S_{yy}}=\underbrace{\sum(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}_{SS_R=\hat\beta_1S_{xy}}+\underbrace{\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}_{SS_E},
with degrees of freedom $n-1=1+(n-2)$.

Write $y_i-\bar{y}=(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})+(y_i-\hat{y}_i)$ and square. The cross term is $2\sum(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})e_i=2\hat\beta_1\sum(x_i-\bar{x})e_i=0$. The normal equations make the residuals sum to zero and be orthogonal to the $x_i$.
The ratio of the mean squares gives an $F$-test that is equivalent to the $t$-test.

Let $MS_R=SS_R/1$ and $MS_E=SS_E/(n-2)$. When $H_0:\beta_1=0$ is true, $F_0=MS_R/MS_E\sim F_{1,\,n-2}$. Reject $H_0$ if $f_0>f_{\alpha,\,1,\,n-2}$. Also $F_0=T_0^2$, where $T_0=\hat\beta_1/\se(\hat\beta_1)$.
The $t$-test is more flexible than the $F$-test: it also allows one-sided alternatives.
Confidence Intervals on the Slope and Intercept
Two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ intervals:
slope: $\hat\beta_1\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$;
intercept: $\hat\beta_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})}$;
variance: $\dfrac{(n-2)\hat\sigma^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}}\le\sigma^2\le\dfrac{(n-2)\hat\sigma^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}}$.
One-sided versions. Use $\alpha$ in one tail and write one limit only.
Slope, upper bound: $\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+t_{\alpha,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$.
Slope, lower bound: $\hat\beta_1-t_{\alpha,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}\le\beta_1$. The intercept is similar.
Variance: $\sigma^2\le(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{1-\alpha,\,n-2}$ and $\sigma^2\ge(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{\alpha,\,n-2}$.
Matching tests: reject $H_1:\beta_1>\beta_{1,0}$ when $t_0>t_{\alpha,\,n-2}$; reject $H_1:\beta_1<\beta_{1,0}$ when $t_0<-t_{\alpha,\,n-2}$.
The end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval is a one-sided $97.5\%$ bound, not a one-sided $95\%$ bound.
The same applies to the intervals on the mean response and the prediction interval below: use $t_{\alpha,\,n-2}$ and keep one limit.
Confidence Interval on the Mean Response

The mean response at $x=x_0$ is $\mu_{Y|x_0}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0$. It is estimated by $\hat\mu_{Y|x_0}=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0$. This estimator is normal and unbiased, with variance $\sigma^2\Big[\dfrac1n+\dfrac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]$.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval on $\mu_{Y|x_0}$ is
\hat\mu_{Y|x_0}\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\Big[\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]}.

The interval is narrowest at $x_0=\bar{x}$ and widens as $x_0$ moves away from the centre of the data. We know the line best in the middle. The confidence level applies to one chosen $x_0$, not to the whole line.
A new observation $Y_0$ at $x_0$ equals the mean response plus a new error $\varepsilon_0$, independent of the data.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval for a future observation $Y_0$ at $x_0$ is
\hat{y}_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\Big[1+\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]}.
$Y_0-\hat{Y}_0$ has mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2+\sigma^2[1/n+(x_0-\bar{x})^2/S_{xx}]$. The two parts are independent. Standardising with $\hat\sigma$ gives a $t_{n-2}$ pivot.
This is much wider than the $\pm0.160$ for the mean response. Even if the line were known exactly, one new observation still scatters by $\sigma$.
The tests and intervals are valid only if the model assumptions hold: a linear relationship, independent errors with constant variance, and (for small $n$) normal errors.
Residual Analysis
The residual is $e_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i$. The standardised residual is $d_i=e_i/\hat\sigma$. If the model is correct, about $95\%$ of the $d_i$ lie within $\pm2$.
A point far outside $\pm2$ may be an outlier. But outliers can carry important information, so do not discard them automatically.
Graphical checks:
Normal probability plot of residuals. Points near a line support normality. Curvature means skew or heavy tails.

Residuals against fitted values (or against $x$). A random horizontal band is good. A curve means the line is the wrong shape: try a quadratic term or a transformation. A funnel (spread grows with $\hat{y}$) means non-constant variance: transform the response ($\sqrt{y}$, $\ln y$ or $1/y$), or use weighted least squares.
Residuals against time order. Runs of residuals with the same sign mean correlated errors.
Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$)
R^2=\frac{SS_R}{SS_T}=1-\frac{SS_E}{SS_T},\qquad 0\le R^2\le1.
It is the proportion of the variability in $y$ explained by the regression.
Cautions:
$R^2$ does not measure the size of the slope. A large $R^2$ does not mean a steep line.
A large $R^2$ does not prove the linear model is correct. A curved relationship over a short range can give $R^2$ near $1$.
A small $R^2$ is not necessarily bad: the noise may simply be large.
$R^2$ never decreases when you add terms. You can reach $R^2=1$ with a polynomial of degree $n-1$. So $R^2$ cannot compare models of different size (see Chapter 6).
Lack-of-Fit Test (CD Only)
If some $x$ values have repeated observations (replicates), split the error sum of squares into pure error and lack of fit:
SS_E=SS_{PE}+SS_{LOF},
SS_{PE}=\sum_i\sum_j(y_{ij}-\bar{y}_i)^2\ \ (n-m\text{ df}),\qquad SS_{LOF}=SS_E-SS_{PE}\ \ (m-2\text{ df}),
where $m$ is the number of distinct $x$ values. If the straight line is adequate,
F_0=\frac{SS_{LOF}/(m-2)}{SS_{PE}/(n-m)}\sim F_{m-2,\,n-m}.
A large $F_0$ is evidence of curvature.
If a scatter plot is clearly curved, transform $x$, $y$ or both so the relationship becomes linear. Then use the methods above.
Two cautions:

A transformation changes the error structure as well as the mean. If $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}\varepsilon$ with a multiplicative error, then $\ln y$ has an additive error, and the log-linear fit is correct. If the original error is additive, the log-transformed errors do not have constant variance. Always re-check the residuals after transforming.
A prediction made on the transformed scale (for example of $\ln y$) must be back-transformed. The back-transformed mean of $\ln y$ estimates the median of $y$, not its mean.

To stabilise variance, use $\sqrt y$ for counts, and $\ln y$ when the standard deviation is proportional to the mean. The Box–Cox family $y^{(\lambda)}=(y^\lambda-1)/\lambda$ picks $\lambda$ by maximum likelihood.
So far $x$ was a fixed regressor. Now suppose $(X,Y)$ are both random, with a bivariate normal distribution, and we want the strength of their linear association.
The population correlation is $\rho=\dfrac{\Cov(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\in[-1,1]$. The sample correlation coefficient is
R=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}=\hat\beta_1\sqrt{\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{yy}}}.
Facts:
$R^2$ equals the coefficient of determination of Section 5.8.2.
$R$ has the same sign as $\hat\beta_1$, and $\hat\beta_1=R\,s_y/s_x$.
$R=\pm1$ if and only if all points lie exactly on a line.
If $(X,Y)$ is bivariate normal:
To test $H_0:\rho=0$, use $T_0=\dfrac{R\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-R^2}}\sim t_{n-2}$. This is identical to the $t$-test of $H_0:\beta_1=0$.

For other hypotheses and for intervals, use Fisher’s transformation. $Z=\tfrac12\ln\dfrac{1+R}{1-R}=\operatorname{arctanh}R$ is approximately $\Normal\Big(\operatorname{arctanh}\rho,\ \dfrac1{n-3}\Big)$. A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for $\rho$ is $\tanh\big(\operatorname{arctanh}r\pm z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{n-3}\big)$.
For the example data, $r=\sqrt{0.9988}=0.9994$. Then $t_0=0.9994\sqrt6/\sqrt{1-0.9988}=70.7$, which matches the regression $t$ up to rounding.
For an interval with $n=20$ and $r=0.6$: $\operatorname{arctanh}0.6=0.693$. So $0.693\pm1.96/\sqrt{17}=0.693\pm0.475$, and $\rho\in(\tanh0.218,\ \tanh1.168)=(0.21,\ 0.82)$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Wire bond pull strength against wire length

blocks.x: $n=25$ bonds, $S_{xx}=698.56$, $S_{xy}=2027.7132$. Then $r=0.9818$ and $r^2=0.9640$: wire length explains $96.4\%$ of the variability in pull strength.

Test $H_0:\rho=\rho_0$ with $\rho_0\ne0$ (moderate $n\ge25$). Use $z_0=(\operatorname{arctanh}r-\operatorname{arctanh}\rho_0)\sqrt{n-3}$. Reject if $\abs{z_0}>z_{\alpha/2}$ (or $z_\alpha$ for a one-sided test).

Interval. $\operatorname{arctanh}0.9818=2.3452$, so the $95\%$ interval is $\tanh(2.3452\pm1.96/\sqrt{22})=\tanh(1.927,\ 2.763)$, that is, $0.958\le\rho\le0.992$. A one-sided $95\%$ lower bound uses $1.645$ in place of $1.96$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: correlation is not causation, and zero correlation is not independence

blocks.x: A high correlation can come from a common cause, or from coincidence.
Correlation measures linear association only. If $X$ is symmetric about zero and $Y=X^2$, then $\rho=0$, yet $Y$ is a function of $X$.
One outlier can create or destroy a large correlation. Always look at the scatter plot. Anscombe’s quartet has four very different data sets with the same $r=0.816$ and the same regression line.

Model: $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$. Least squares: $\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$, $\hat\sigma^2=SS_E/(n-2)$, with $SS_E=S_{yy}-\hat\beta_1S_{xy}$.
$\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})$. The estimators are BLUE (Gauss–Markov).
Tests and intervals use $t_{n-2}$. Test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ also by $F_0=MS_R/MS_E=t_0^2$, with $SS_T=SS_R+SS_E$.
Mean response: $\hat{y}_0\pm t\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2[1/n+(x_0-\bar{x})^2/S_{xx}]}$. For a new observation add $1$ inside the bracket. Both are narrowest at $\bar{x}$.
Check the residuals (normal plot, plot against $\hat{y}$). $R^2=SS_R/SS_T$. Lack of fit needs replicates. Transformations can linearise some curves.
$r=S_{xy}/\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$ and $t_0=r\sqrt{n-2}/\sqrt{1-r^2}$. Fisher’s $z$ gives intervals for $\rho$.

For the data $x$: $2,4,5,7,9,10$ and $y$: $5.1,8.3,9.8,14.2,18.0,19.6$, find the least squares line, $\hat\sigma^2$, the $95\%$ confidence interval for the slope, and test $H_0:\beta_1=2$ against $\beta_1\ne2$.
Construct the analysis of variance table for the data of Exercise 1 and test the significance of regression with $\alpha=0.05$. Verify $F_0=t_0^2$ and compute $R^2$.

Using Exercise 1, find a $95\%$ confidence interval on the mean response at $x_0=6$ and a $95\%$ prediction interval for a new observation at $x_0=6$. Why is the second wider? What happens at $x_0=20$?
Prove that the residuals of a least squares line with an intercept satisfy $\sum e_i=0$ and $\sum x_ie_i=0$, and deduce that the fitted line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$.
Show that $\hat\beta_1=R\,s_y/s_x$ and $R^2=SS_R/SS_T$. If $R=0.8$ and $s_y=10$, $s_x=2$, find $\hat\beta_1$ and the proportion of variance explained.
The data below follow an approximate relationship $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}$: $x=1,2,3,4,5$; $y=2.7,7.1,20.5,54.9,148.0$. Linearise, fit by least squares and estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$.
In a sample of $n=27$ pairs $r=-0.45$. Test $H_0:\rho=0$ and find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\rho$ using Fisher’s transformation.
Explain, with the help of a residual plot sketch, how to recognise (a) a nonlinear relationship, (b) non-constant variance and (c) a single outlier, and what you would do about each.
